To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

the Lesser grey shrike is declining in several peripheral populations in the Mediterranean area, and the interannual fluctuation of these populations are spatially correlated, suggesting that they are responding to a common factor.
(1) the Lesser grey shrikes are declining in the study area, (2) the populations are strongly synchronized in their dynamics and (3) there is evidence of climate change in the breeding area.
the Lesser grey shrike populations in France and northeast Spain are spatially synchronized in their population trend.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the population trends and the spatial synchrony in a peripheral bird species in relation with environmental changes and their implications for conservation.
the population dynamics of the Lesser grey shrike, a species with a declining population trend and a restricted range in Europe and with a large part of its range at the western border.
the study of a peripheral population and its consequences on the conservation status of this endangered bird species.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that

, although the Lesser grey shrike is not yet a threatened species in Europe (it is classified as Least Concern), it is a species in need of urgent conservation actions in southern France and northeastern Spain.
environmental change is affecting some peripheral populations of the lesser grey shrike, and this may be influencing the decline of the whole western population of the species.

the Lesser grey shrike populations at the western limit are declining in numbers, and that this decline is related to the climate change in their breeding and wintering areas, but further studies are needed in order to ascertain the causal relationship between climate change and the decline in numbers of Lesser grey shrikes in Europe and North Africa.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
climate change is affecting the dynamics of some peripheral populations of Lesser grey shrikes and this effect may be transmitted to neighboring populations.

the spatial synchrony of the studied peripheral populations of the Lesser grey shrike, together with the evidence of climatic changes in their breeding areas, could be a key element to account for their population trends and therefore a useful approach to understand the causes of their decline.
climate change could be a major threat for the Lesser grey shrike and that conservation measures should be applied at the scale of the western Mediterranean basin.
The main takeaway from our work is that
climate change may be a threat to peripheral populations, and that conservation efforts should include the study of the environmental changes in the breeding area.

climate change may have a significant effect on the dynamics and distribution of peripheral populations, so that the conservation of these populations should be considered in the management of the species.
the study of the dynamics of peripheral populations of endangered species may provide important clues on the causes of their decline, which can be crucial for the design of conservation strategies.
